lead: The A320 and the B787 sit at opposite ends of civil power-system design. The A320 keeps a fixed-frequency 115 V AC supply at 400 Hz and a 28 V DC supply from transformer rectifiers. The B787 is a more-electric, bleedless aircraft: 235 V AC at variable frequency and ±270 V DC. Higher voltage means less current for the same power, so thinner, lighter cables and lower copper loss. Comparing the two shows how voltage, frequency and conversion choices fit together into one architecture.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for generation and protection, 3.2 for conversion, and 3.11 for bus arrangements.

sections.h3: A320: fixed frequency, two voltage levels

blocks.text: The A320 has two engine-driven integrated drive generators (IDGs), each rated 90 kVA at 115/200 V, 400 Hz. The rating is in kVA, apparent power, not kW. Each IDG has a generator control unit (GCU) that regulates its field, watches for faults and closes its generator line contactor onto its own AC bus, AC BUS 1 or AC BUS 2. The buses are split in normal flight; a bus tie contactor joins them when one generator is off, so this is the split-parallel scheme of bus systems.

The APU generator, also 90 kVA, can replace either IDG on the ground or in flight, and ground power plugs in at the nose. Two transformer rectifiers (TR 1 and TR 2, 200 A each) make 28 V DC for DC BUS 1 and DC BUS 2, and an essential TR feeds the essential DC bus when needed. Two nickel-cadmium batteries start the APU and hold the essential buses for short gaps, and a static inverter makes AC for the essential AC bus from battery power. If all AC is lost, the RAT drives the blue hydraulic system, and a hydraulic-motor-driven emergency generator of about 5 kVA feeds the essential buses (see emergency power).

sections.h3: B787: variable frequency and more electric

blocks.text: The B787 takes no bleed air from its engines. Cabin pressurisation, wing ice protection, the brakes and several hydraulic pumps run on electricity instead, so it needs far more electrical power. Each engine carries two variable-frequency starter-generators (VFSGs), four in all, each rated 250 kVA. A starter-generator starts the engine as a motor and then generates. With no constant-speed drive, the output is 235 V AC at a frequency of about 360 Hz to 800 Hz that follows engine speed. Two APU starter-generators of 225 kVA each add backup, so the total installed generation is 4 × 250 + 2 × 225 = 1450 kVA. The four main generators alone give 1000 kVA, more than five times the 180 kVA of the A320's two IDGs.

Conversion is spread out. Auto-transformer rectifier units (ATRUs) turn 235 V AC into ±270 V DC for the big motor controllers (cabin compressors, hydraulic pumps, engine start), auto-transformer units (ATUs) make 115 V AC for older-style loads, and TRUs make 28 V DC. Small loads are switched by solid-state power controllers in remote power distribution units near the loads. Lithium-ion main and APU batteries start the APU and hold the DC buses, and the RAT powers the essential buses when all normal sources fail. Every load on the variable-frequency bus must accept the whole 360 to 800 Hz range; that is the key design rule of the aircraft.

blocks.where: P is real power in watts; V<sub>ph</sub> is the phase (line-to-neutral) voltage, the 115 V or 235 V quoted for aircraft systems; I is the line current in amperes; cos φ is the power factor. The same power is √3 × V<sub>LL</sub> × I × cos φ, with V<sub>LL</sub> = √3 × V<sub>ph</sub> (200 V and 407 V).

blocks.text: At unity power factor I = P ÷ (3 V<sub>ph</sub>). Copper loss in a three-phase cable is 3 I<sup>2</sup> R, where R is the resistance of one conductor. For the same power, raising the voltage lowers the current in proportion and the loss as 1 ÷ V<sup>2</sup>. That is why 235 V AC and ±270 V DC save copper weight, but they demand new insulation, connectors and arc protection.

examples.question: A 100 kW balanced three-phase load at unity power factor is fed first from a 115 V (line-to-neutral) system and then from a 235 V (line-to-neutral) system, through the same cable. Find the line current in each case and the ratio of cable copper loss.
steps: Given: P = 100 kW = 100 000 W; V<sub>ph1</sub> = 115 V; V<sub>ph2</sub> = 235 V; cos φ = 1.
Check with the line voltage: V<sub>LL</sub> = 1.732 × 115 = 199.2 V, and 100 000 ÷ (1.732 × 199.2) = 289.9 A, the same.
The cable is the same, so R is the same and the loss 3 I<sup>2</sup> R scales with I<sup>2</sup>: ratio = (289.9 ÷ 141.8)<sup>2</sup> = 2.044<sup>2</sup> = 4.18.
The same ratio comes straight from the voltages: (235 ÷ 115)<sup>2</sup> = 4.18.
examples.answer: The line current is 289.9 A at 115 V and 141.8 A at 235 V, so the 235 V system has 1/4.18 of the copper loss, or it can use a thinner, lighter cable for the same loss.

traps: Do not say the B787 needs a constant-speed drive. Its AC bus is variable frequency by design; every load must accept 360-800 Hz.
Do not mix 235 V AC with ±270 V DC. The first is generated and distributed as AC; the second is made from it by ATRUs for large motor loads.
The A320's 115 V is fixed at 400 Hz because the IDG holds generator speed constant; the engine speed itself is not constant.
Generator ratings in kVA are apparent power, not kW. At a power factor below one, the kW available is lower than the kVA rating.
The RAT is an emergency source, not a normal source for engine start or ground power.
Putting 115 V into √3 × V × I. Aircraft quote line-to-neutral voltage: use 3 × 115 × I, or √3 × 200 × I.

quiz.q: State the A320 main AC generator rating, voltage and frequency.
quiz.a: 90 kVA, 115 V AC (line-to-neutral), 400 Hz, one IDG per engine.

quiz.q: What DC bus voltage does the B787 make from its TRUs?
Why does the B787 not need a constant-speed drive?
quiz.a: The generator output is allowed to vary in frequency with engine speed (360-800 Hz); loads are designed to accept that range, so no fixed-speed gearbox is needed.

quiz.q: A balanced three-phase 50 kW load at unity power factor is fed from the B787's 235 V (line-to-neutral) bus. Find the line current.
For the same cable and same real power, compare copper loss at 115 V and 235 V.
quiz.a: Loss scales as 1 ÷ V<sup>2</sup> for the same power and cable, so the ratio is (235 ÷ 115)<sup>2</sup> = 4.18: the 235 V case has about a quarter of the loss.

quiz.q: Why is a variable-frequency bus a system-wide design rule, not just a generator change?
quiz.a: Every load, transformer, motor and power supply connected to that bus must tolerate 360-800 Hz; otherwise it may overheat, lose regulation or fail.

quiz.q: How is DC made from the AC buses in each aircraft?
quiz.a: A320: transformer rectifiers turn 115 V AC into 28 V DC. B787: ATRUs turn 235 V AC into ±270 V DC, and TRUs make 28 V DC.

beyond: Not for the exam. More-electric aircraft research pushes voltage higher to cut cable weight and power bleedless cabins, electric brakes and electric engine accessories. Wide-bandgap devices such as silicon carbide and gallium nitride make high-voltage DC conversion lighter. Search for more electric aircraft, variable frequency AC power and ±270 V DC distribution.
